woodlouse.note: Woodlouse, pill bug (Isopoda, Oniscidea): about twenty facets to an eye, so no picture, only light and from where. The same picture as the other entry.
woodlouse.cue: Hold the phone close to the ground and turn it slowly. A woodlouse heads for the darker side.

field.note: inferred from facet counts; no resolution is measured in a woodlouse

rows: Two small-eyed water isopods have 4 and about 25 facets to an eye, and a close picture of a Rough Woodlouse’s eye shows 22. The Asian shore crab has 2,400 to 6,000.
The sea slater, a big-eyed seashore relative, has facets about 7 degrees apart, which resolves about 0.07 cycles per degree, near an eight-hundredth of your 60.
With about twenty facets to an eye, a woodlouse is drawn with no image at all, only how much light there is and from where.
Woodlice turn away from light toward dark shelters, where the air is damper and cooler.
Woodlice shelter more when the air is dry, and huddled together they lose about half as much water as they do alone.
About six in ten Common Pill Woodlice are active at night, against nine in ten of Philoscia muscorum, the fourth most recorded woodlouse.
No measurement of a woodlouse’s colour sense was found, so the picture is grey.
How far and how evenly a woodlouse walks changes with the dampness of the air, which a camera cannot show.

horseshoe.note: Horseshoe crab, sketched for later in the sheet.

docs/views/sheets/crab.md#2 horseshoe Colour: Chapman and Lall 1967; Battelle 2014

rows: Each eye on the side of the shell has about a thousand facets and takes in about 60 per cent of the half of the world on its side.
On average it resolves 0.1 cycles per degree, a six-hundredth of yours, and up to 0.22 toward the front.
A clock in its brain makes its eyes up to 100,000 times more sensitive at night, and it finds mates by sight by day and by night.
Those eyes have a single peak of sensitivity near 520 nanometres, and no colour vision has been found, so the picture is grey.
Its small eye on top of the shell responds to ultraviolet 200 to 320 times more strongly than to visible light, and a phone camera keeps little of that light.
No source describes a pupil in a horseshoe crab's eye, so none is drawn.

notes.why: A fiddler crab resolves vertical detail about five times finer than horizontal (0.25 against 1.33 degrees). The engine blurs the same in both directions. Easy with a new blur.

Two streaks at the horizon (Bagheri 2020) and a band held level on a slope (Zeil 1990). topoS draws one band at the horizon; the sheet leaves it unset because 15 percent of decapod records are measured without the band.
The eye about a thousand times more sensitive at night (Brodrick 2022): the clock could raise gain and lower rate after dark. Easy, but the size of the lift would be invented.
Polarization contrast on mud and water. No phone input records it.
Horseshoe crab: two windows aimed sideways, each about 60 percent of its half of the world. The aperture mask could take a two-window shape.

rows: A fiddler crab’s eyes stand on tall stalks and see the whole way around. The picture is squeezed and bent to suggest that.
From side to side a fiddler crab’s facets point about 1.3 degrees apart, so it resolves about 0.4 cycles per degree to your 60.

Fiddler and ghost crabs see up-and-down detail more finely in a thin band along the horizon, about five times finer than side-to-side detail in one fiddler crab, and a ghost crab keeps that band on the horizon even on a slope. They make up about one decapod record in twelve, and the families measured without the band make up more, so it is not drawn.
Most light cells in a crab’s eye share one pigment, most sensitive to blue-green near 500 nanometres, so reds go dark. Female fiddler crabs still pick a yellow claw over a grey one of any brightness.

Female fiddler crabs prefer males whose claws reflect ultraviolet. A phone lens that was tested let through between a fifth and a hundredth of it, and the picture cannot pick it out, so the sheen here is invented.
In daylight a fiddler crab’s eye follows flicker to about 74 a second, a little past your 60. Once its eye has adapted to the dark, it follows only about 35 to 40.
At night a fiddler crab’s dark-adapted eye answers to light about a thousand times dimmer than the same dark-adapted eye does by day.
Crayfish and slipper lobsters have superposition eyes, a design suited to dim water. A crayfish has one set of light cells most sensitive to violet and another most sensitive to yellow.
A fiddler crab tells apart polarized light whose angle differs by 3 degrees, and uses it to pick out objects on the mud. A phone camera does not record polarization, so it is left out.

rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: If you are a green shore crab, a review lists your sharpness at about half a cycle a degree, a sixtieth of the 30 cycles a degree a human reads on an eye chart. If you are a horned ghost crab, the same review lists under 2 cycles a degree, about a twentieth of a human's. Nobody has measured how sharply you see if you are a Dungeness crab, a Sally Lightfoot crab or a northern kelp crab, among many others.
rows.note: Left out the blue crab's 1.8 degree figure (R30) because it is an angle, and no record converts it to cycles a degree. Rounded the horned ghost crab's 1.57 to "under 2".

rows.title: The horizon
rows.text: If you are a horned ghost crab, a band across each eye level with the horizon is about 30 degrees high, and at its finest your eye samples four times more finely up and down than side to side. The fiddler crab Uca lactea has a band like this too, running around the middle of its eyes. Nobody has measured whether you have one unless you are one of those crabs or a close relative of the ghost crab.
rows.note: Left out the mantis shrimp records (not crabs) and R4, whose quoted value does not state a horizon band.

rows.title: Color
rows.text: The Asian shore crab has two kinds of color-sensing pigment in its eyes, one for violet-blue light and one for blue-green light, and you very likely have two as well. A review lists two kinds in the red swamp crawfish too. In the larger light-sensing cells of four fiddler crab species, only one kind was found.

cites.taxon: Uca pugnax, U. pugilator, U. vomeris, U. tangeri

rows.note: Replaced "reports" with "lists" for the voice check. Left out the crawfish peak numbers because the table gives "560/600" without explaining it.

rows.title: Ultraviolet
rows.text: The shore crab Hemigrapsus sanguineus has one kind of color-sensing cell that peaks in violet-blue light, at about 440 nanometers, and one that peaks in green, at about 510. Four fiddler crab species have a single kind of cell, peaking between 510 and 530. Nobody has measured whether you have a cell that senses ultraviolet, the light just beyond violet.

cites.taxon: Uca pugnax, U. pugilator, U. vomeris, U. tangeri

rows.note: No record gives a crab cell peaking below 400 nm, so the row states the gap. Mantis shrimp UV records (R4, R13) left out because they are not crabs.

rows.title: Pace
rows.text: Nobody has measured how fast a light can flash before you stop seeing it flicker, and that is true for most crabs. If you are a Dampier's fiddler crab, your eyes follow a flicker of about 75 flashes a second by day and about 60 at night, where a human stops at about 60. A review lists 14 flashes a second for the deep-sea crab Bathynectes longipes.
rows.note: No flicker measurement exists in the records for the commonly met crabs, so the row names only two measured crabs.

rows.title: Night
rows.text: If you are a Dampier's fiddler crab, your eyes are far more sensitive at night, and the dimmest flash that gives an electrical signal from your eye is about a thousand times dimmer than the one needed by day. Nobody has measured how dim a light you can see if you are most other crabs, crayfish or shrimp.
rows.note: Left out R2 and R3: their figures are calculated from eye dimensions in other species, and numbers do not travel.

rows.title: Crayfish
rows.text: Nobody has recorded what kind of eye you have if you are a red swamp crawfish, a signal crayfish or a yabby. A review says that many adult crabs keep apposition eyes, and an anatomical study found that slipper lobsters have a superposition eye with square facets. Nobody has checked whether a crayfish eye matches either one.
rows.note: Replaced "reports" with "says". R1's value text mentions reflecting eyes in shrimps, but its quote does not state it, so I left it out.

rows.title: Polarized light
rows.text: Polarized light is light whose waves vibrate in one direction, and fiddler crabs, mantis shrimp and the tawny hermit crab have all been shown to see it. The tawny hermit crab and two other hermit crabs spotted predator-like shapes by polarization contrast alone. If you are not one of the crabs that were tested, nobody has measured whether you see it.

cites.taxon: Coenobita rugosus and two other hermit crabs

rows.note: Left out the common mud crab result (R5, gaze steadied by brightness cues) and the signal crayfish anatomy (R7, suggestion only).
